title: How to Build a Talent Retention Plan (September 2026)
summary: Cut startup turnover with retention tactics covering compensation, onboarding, and growth that work for small teams. September 2026.
body_markdown:
Most startups don’t have a real[talent retention strategy](https://www.dover.com/) until after someone important leaves. Then it becomes urgent. But turnover is rarely random, and the patterns that predict it tend to show up well before anyone’s calendar is cleared out. What follows is a practical look at what actually drives people to stay, and what you can do about it before it becomes a problem.


**TLDR:**


-


Replacing one employee can cost 50% to 200% of their annual salary, making retention a core financial decision.


-


Track retention rate quarterly by team and tenure band, instead of company-wide at year-end alone.


-


The top drivers of voluntary turnover are compensation gaps, weak onboarding, and no visible growth path.


-


Stay interviews run quarterly per employee to catch flight risk signals that no survey tool surfaces on its own.


-


When turnover does happen, an ATS keeps the pipeline intact so backfilling doesn’t start from scratch, and on-demand recruiting support can layer in for senior or hard-to-fill roles without a full-time recruiter on staff.


## Why Talent Retention Is a Startup’s Most Expensive Blind Spot


Most startups track burn rate obsessively but rarely track the cost of losing people. That gap compounds fast.


[Voluntary turnover costs $1 trillion annually](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx) , and[replacement costs 50% to 200% of salary](https://www.qooper.io/blog/cost-of-employee-turnover) depending on seniority. For a startup losing a $120,000 engineer, that’s anywhere from $60,000 to $240,000 in recruiting, onboarding, and lost productivity before the new hire is fully contributing.


Institutional knowledge walks out with that person. Team morale dips. Remaining employees notice. A strong[talent retention strategy](https://www.dover.com/blog/talent-retention-strategies-keep-best-employees) treats this as a core business problem, not a quarterly HR metric.


## What Talent Retention Actually Means


Employee retention measures what percentage of your team chose to stay over a given period. That number tells you something the hiring funnel can’t: how the actual experience of working at your company holds up over time.


A few terms get conflated here. Retention rate and turnover rate are mirror metrics: one tracks who stayed, the other who left. Engagement is related but distinct: it measures how invested people feel in their work, while retention measures whether they stuck around. High engagement tends to support retention, but engaged employees still leave when compensation or growth opportunities fall short.


Voluntary and involuntary turnover signal different things. Voluntary turnover usually points to unmet expectations: compensation gaps, limited career growth, or a manager relationship that broke down. Involuntary turnover reflects business conditions or[early-stage startup hiring decisions](https://www.dover.com/blog/top-hiring-practices-every-early-stage-startup-should-know) . A retention strategy worth building pays attention to both, because high involuntary turnover can mask a hiring problem as easily as a culture one.


## How to Calculate Your Employee Retention Rate


The formula is straightforward:


**(Employees at end of period / Employees at start of period) x 100**


If you started the year with 40 people and ended with 35, your retention rate is 87.5%. That number becomes meaningful when you track it consistently and segment it by department, tenure, or role level. A 90% company-wide rate can hide a 60% rate on your engineering team.[Recruiting metrics problems](https://www.dover.com/blog/common-problems-with-recruiting-metrics-how-to-avoid-them) like this appear when data is read at too high a level.


Most growing startups aim for 85% or higher annually. Rates below 80% usually signal something structural: compensation misalignment, weak onboarding, or a management problem worth investigating before adding headcount.


Run this calculation quarterly, beyond the year-end check-in. Early signals give you room to respond before a pattern becomes a crisis.


## Why Employees Leave: The Real Drivers of Turnover


Turnover rarely comes from nowhere. According to[Paycor’s employee retention research](https://www.paycor.com/resource-center/articles/employee-retention-statistics/) , 51% of employees are actively seeking new opportunities right now, and 42% of turnover is considered preventable. Nearly half of departures happen for reasons a company could have acted on.


The persistent drivers are consistent across industries:


Driver Warning sign First move


Compensation below market Offers rejected; candidates counter well above your range Benchmark base and total comp against Levels.fyi or Radford annually


Manager quality Direct reports avoid 1:1s; feedback arrives only at reviews Train managers on regular, specific feedback cadences


No visible growth path Strong performers ask about promotions with no clear answer Write career ladders; discuss them in quarterly check-ins


Weak onboarding New hires still unclear on expectations at 60 days Set written 30-60-90 day goals before the start date


Employees rarely leave over a single bad day. They leave after a series of unmet needs go unacknowledged long enough that another offer becomes the easier decision.


## Competitive Compensation and Benefits That Actually Retain People


Salary is the baseline, but rarely the whole story. Employees compare offers on total compensation: base, equity, health coverage, retirement, and whatever else fills the gap between similar-paying roles.


Start with benchmarking. Tools like Levels.fyi, Radford, and Glassdoor let you check where your offers land relative to market. If base salaries sit consistently 15-20% below competitors, no amount of culture investment closes that gap.


Equity matters more at startups than anywhere else, but only if employees understand what they hold. Explain vesting schedules, dilution, and rough scenarios in plain language. Perceived value collapses when people don’t understand the math.


For teams with tighter budgets, high-perceived-value benefits often cost less than a salary adjustment:


-


Fully covered health insurance, even a modest plan, beats a high-deductible one where employees absorb premiums out of pocket


-


A learning stipend in the $500-$1,000 per year range is low cost and signals real investment in growth


-


Extra PTO or a flexible schedule carries outsized perceived value relative to its cost


-


Remote work flexibility has become a retention factor in roles where it’s feasible


The employees most likely to stay aren’t always chasing the highest number. They’re looking for transparency about how pay decisions get made and confidence that the structure is fair.


## Onboarding as a Retention Lever


Most turnover happens quietly, and earlier than most founders expect. Employees who feel lost in their first few months rarely announce frustration. They start passively searching.


Structured onboarding reduces that risk. The first 90 days set an employee’s baseline assumptions: what’s expected of them, whether the role matches what they were sold, and whether their manager has time for them. How that transition feels begins with[candidate experience best practices](https://www.dover.com/blog/candidate-experience-guide-best-practices) during the hiring process itself. When those assumptions go negative early, the exit timeline compresses.


A retention-focused onboarding program covers a few things most startups skip:


-


Clear 30-60-90 day goals written before the start date, not improvised after


-


An assigned peer or buddy beyond just the direct manager


-


Explicit context about how the team operates: how decisions get made, what good work looks like, and where the role sits in the bigger picture


-


A structured check-in at 30 days to surface confusion before it calcifies


Motivation problems that surface at month six often trace back to ambiguity planted in week two. The fix is a process run consistently every time someone new joins.


## Career Growth, Internal Mobility, and Development Programs


Perceived stagnation kills retention faster than almost any other factor. High performers leave when the ceiling feels close, and at a startup, that ceiling can appear surprisingly early if no one has mapped out what growth looks like beyond the next six months.


Career pathing doesn’t require an elaborate HR system. It requires a direct conversation about where someone could go, what getting there looks like, and what the company is willing to invest. Written career ladders help, but a manager who actively discusses them matters more.


Concrete development programs that retain people:


-


Funded external learning: conferences, online courses, certifications, or degree programs with a clear reimbursement policy


-


Internal promotion cycles with transparent criteria, so employees aren’t guessing why someone else got the role


-


Cross-functional projects that let people build skills outside their current lane without a formal transfer


-


Mentorship pairings, whether internal or through external networks, for employees who want structured guidance


When a strong performer wants a different role, losing them to that role internally costs almost nothing. Losing them to a competitor costs everything. Companies that treat internal movement as a threat tend to have higher voluntary turnover than those that treat it as a retention tool.


## Building a Culture That Keeps People


Culture is one of those words that gets used to mean anything convenient. Here it means something specific: the daily environment that determines whether people feel safe, valued, and like their work matters.


Manager quality sits at the center of this. Research consistently shows that people leave managers, not companies. A retention strategy that invests in leadership development, structured feedback training, and clear expectations for how managers engage with their teams will outperform one that relies on office perks.


Psychological safety, the degree to which people believe they can raise concerns or push back without consequences, has a direct impact on whether strong performers stay engaged or quietly start looking. Teams where people self-censor tend to have higher voluntary turnover among the employees most likely to find a better environment elsewhere.


A few cultural conditions that separate high-retention environments from low-retention ones:


-


Managers who give direct, regular feedback instead of saving everything for annual reviews


-


Decision-making transparency, including the reasoning behind choices that affect people’s work


-


DE&I commitments that show up in hiring, pay equity audits, and promotion rates, beyond a stated value


-


Recognition practices that are specific and timely, because the absence of acknowledgment is itself a message


-


A genuine policy on how conflict gets handled when it surfaces


Culture retains people by removing the friction and inequity that makes leaving feel like relief.

## FAQs


### What’s a realistic employee retention rate target for an early-stage startup?


Most growing startups aim for 85% or higher annually, with rates below 80% typically pointing to a structural issue worth investigating before adding headcount. For the full formula and how to segment results by team, see the ‘How to Calculate Your Employee Retention Rate’ section above.


### How do you build an employee retention plan without a dedicated HR team?


Start with a simple tracking document that captures your current retention rate by department and tenure band, flags high-risk segments (employees in their first 12 months and those approaching two to three years tend to show the highest voluntary departure risk), and assigns manager ownership over stay interviews on a defined schedule. Written interventions should connect to diagnosed causes: early attrition usually traces back to onboarding gaps, while mid-tenure departures more often point to compensation or growth. They should not be drawn from a general list of perks.


### Do I need a recruiter if I already have an ATS for backfilling roles?


An ATS manages pipeline; a fractional recruiting agency handles sourcing. For roles with strong inbound interest, an ATS alone can be sufficient. For senior, specialized, or low-inbound roles, the bottleneck is sourcing capacity, not pipeline software, and that’s where a fractional recruiting agency working inside the same ATS closes the gap, without the overhead of a full-time hire or the placement-fee misalignment of a contingency firm. Dover’s marketplace connects you with vetted recruiters who carry verified reviews, so you can evaluate fit before the engagement starts.


## Final Thoughts on Talent Retention at Growing Startups


A strong[talent retention strategy](https://www.dover.com/) doesn’t require a dedicated HR team or a complex program. The companies with the lowest turnover pay competitively, set people up well in the first 90 days, and have managers who treat growth conversations as a regular part of the job. Your retention rate is a lagging indicator, but the inputs that drive it, such as compensation, onboarding clarity, career pathing, and psychological safety, are things you can act on now. And when turnover does happen, Dover’s free ATS keeps every candidate pipeline intact so backfilling doesn’t start from scratch, with fractional recruiters available on demand for roles that need more than pipeline software alone.
